topic.title: Graphical-Model Structure and Tractable Inference
topic.area: Graphical Models, Clustering, and Network Structure
topic.overview: Probabilistic graphical models represent dependencies through a graph, making structure central to both interpretation and computation. This topic studies learning that structure, introducing latent variables, and approximating probabilities when exact inference is costly. Special graph families and controlled relaxations can preserve useful dependencies while limiting computational complexity.
topic.whyItMatters: A more expressive graph often makes inference harder, so model design must balance fit with the operations required later. Learning from temporally dependent observations adds another complication: a sequence of updates is not equivalent to independent samples from the equilibrium distribution.
topic.evolution: A 1996 recursive elimination framework maintains probability bounds while approximating general networks. Work in 2013 exploits small feedback vertex sets to make Gaussian-model inference and learning tractable. Recent representatives broaden the observation setting; a 2026 method learns sparse Gaussian conditional-independence graphs from a single Glauber trajectory without a mixing-time-dependent length guarantee.
openQuestions: Which structural restrictions preserve the dependencies most important for prediction?
How much graph information can be recovered before a dependent sampling process mixes?
